In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{S}$:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \textbf{T} & \textbf{S} \\\hline \text{I: Logical schema} & \text{L: Views} \\\hline \text{II: Physical schema} & \text{M: File organization and indexes} \\\hline \text{III: External schema} & \text{N: Relations} \\\hline\end{array}$$
Which one of the following is the correct match from $\mathbf{T}$ to $\mathbf{S}$?
answer_text:
Step‑by‑step matching

Logical schema defines the logical structure of the database, including the tables (relations), attributes, and constraints. It is represented by relations (N).

Physical schema describes how data is stored physically on storage devices, including file organization, indexing strategies, and access methods. It corresponds to file organization and indexes (M).

External schema (also called view schema) defines how end‑users or applications view the data. It consists of views (L).

Thus the correct matching is: I → N, II → M, III → L, which is the third option.
$$\boxed{\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{N},\ \mathrm{II}-\mathrm{M},\ \mathrm{III}-\mathrm{L}}$$

subject: General Aptitude
question:
'When it is raining, peacocks dance.'
Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
When peacocks dance, it is raining.
When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.
answer_text:
The Core Idea: Understanding Logical Implication

This question tests your understanding of the logical structure of conditional statements. The given sentence is a classic "if-then" statement: "If it is raining, then peacocks dance."

In logic, we write this as: $$R \rightarrow D$$
where:
  • $R$ = "It is raining"
  • $D$ = "Peacocks dance"

The key to this question is understanding what necessarily follows from a conditional statement. Many students make the mistake of assuming the converse or inverse is also true, but in logic, only the contrapositive is guaranteed to be true.

The Four Logical Forms

For any conditional statement $R \rightarrow D$, there are four related statements:
  • Original: $R \rightarrow D$ (If it rains, peacocks dance) — Given as true
  • Converse: $D \rightarrow R$ (If peacocks dance, it is raining) — NOT necessarily true
  • Inverse: $\neg R \rightarrow \neg D$ (If it does not rain, peacocks do not dance) — NOT necessarily true
  • Contrapositive: $\neg D \rightarrow \neg R$ (If peacocks do not dance, it is not raining) — ALWAYS true

The contrapositive is the only one that is logically equivalent to the original statement. Let's see why.

Analyzing Each Option

  • Option A: "Peacocks dance only when it is raining."

    This is a common misinterpretation. "Only when" implies that rain is a necessary condition for dancing — peacocks cannot dance without rain. This is the converse of the original statement: $D \rightarrow R$. The original statement only says that rain is a sufficient condition for dancing (if it rains, they will dance). It does not say that rain is the only condition. Peacocks might dance for other reasons as well. So this is not necessarily true.

  • Option B: "When peacocks dance, it is raining."

    This is exactly the converse of the original statement: $D \rightarrow R$. The original statement does not guarantee this. It's possible that peacocks dance when it's sunny, or when they see a lion, or any other reason. The original statement only gives us information about what happens when it rains — it says nothing about what happens when they dance. So this is not necessarily true.

  • Option C: "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining."

    This is the contrapositive of the original statement: $\neg D \rightarrow \neg R$. In logic, the contrapositive of a true statement is always true. If the original statement says that rain always causes dancing, then if you see peacocks not dancing, you can be certain that it is not raining (because if it were raining, they would be dancing). This is the only option that logically follows. CORRECT.

  • Option D: "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance."

    This is the inverse of the original statement: $\neg R \rightarrow \neg D$. The inverse is not logically equivalent to the original. Just because rain causes dancing does not mean the absence of rain causes the absence of dancing. Peacocks could dance for other reasons. So this is not necessarily true.

Summary Table
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Option} & \text{Logical Form} & \text{Equivalent to Original?} & \text{Result} \\ \hline \text{A} & D \rightarrow R \; (\text{Converse}) & \text{No} & \text{INCORRECT} \\ \text{B} & D \rightarrow R \; (\text{Converse}) & \text{No} & \text{INCORRECT} \\ \text{C} & \neg D \rightarrow \neg R \; (\text{Contrapositive}) & \text{Yes} & \text{CORRECT} \\ \text{D} & \neg R \rightarrow \neg D \; (\text{Inverse}) & \text{No} & \text{INCORRECT} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

A Real-World Example

Consider the statement: "If it rains, the ground gets wet." (Rain is sufficient for wet ground.)
  • Does wet ground mean it rained? No — someone could have spilled water. (Converse is false.)
  • If the ground is not wet, does that mean it didn't rain? Yes — if it had rained, the ground would be wet. (Contrapositive is true.)
  • If it doesn't rain, does that mean the ground is not wet? No — someone could still spill water. (Inverse is false.)

Key Takeaway

This question teaches a fundamental rule of logical reasoning:
  • A conditional statement $P \rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg Q \rightarrow \neg P$.
  • The converse ($Q \rightarrow P$) and the inverse ($\neg P \rightarrow \neg Q$) are not logically equivalent to the original statement.

To avoid confusion, remember the phrase: "If P then Q" implies "If not Q then not P" — but it does NOT imply "If Q then P" or "If not P then not Q."

This is one of the most common traps in logical reasoning questions, and now you know exactly how to spot it.

Answer
$$\boxed{\text{When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.}}$$
This corresponds to Option C.

subject: Engineering Mathematics
Operating System
question:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of $1$ MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size $4$ KB. The virtual address space is $64$ GB and physical address space is $1$ GB. If each TLB entry stores a $4$-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a $2$-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)
Note: $1 \mathrm{K}=2^{10}, 1 \mathrm{M}=2^{20}, 1 \mathrm{G}=2^{30}$
answer_text:
Step 1: Understand TLB reach.

TLB reach = Total physical memory accessible via TLB = (Number of TLB entries) $\times$ (Page size).

Given: TLB reach = $1$ MB = $2^{20}$ bytes, Page size = $4$ KB = $2^{12}$ bytes.

Number of TLB entries = $\dfrac{\text{TLB reach}}{\text{Page size}} = \dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{12}} = 2^{8} = 256$ entries.

Step 2: Determine the size of each TLB entry.

Each TLB entry stores:
  • Process ID: $4$ bits
  • Page number: bits required to address a page in the virtual address space
  • Frame number: bits required to address a frame in the physical address space
  • Control field: $2$ bits

Step 3: Calculate bits for page number.

Virtual address space = $64$ GB = $2^{36}$ bytes (since $64 = 2^6$, $1$ GB = $2^{30}$ → $2^6 \times 2^{30} = 2^{36}$).
Page size = $2^{12}$ bytes.

Number of virtual pages = $\dfrac{2^{36}}{2^{12}} = 2^{24}$.
Page number bits = $24$ bits.

Step 4: Calculate bits for frame number.

Physical address space = $1$ GB = $2^{30}$ bytes.
Page size = $2^{12}$ bytes.

Number of physical frames = $\dfrac{2^{30}}{2^{12}} = 2^{18}$.
Frame number bits = $18$ bits.

Step 5: Calculate total bits per TLB entry.

Per entry bits = Process ID ($4$) + Page number ($24$) + Frame number ($18$) + Control ($2$)
= $4 + 24 + 18 + 2 = 48$ bits = $6$ bytes (since $8$ bits = $1$ byte, $48/8 = 6$).

Step 6: Calculate total TLB size.

Number of entries = $256$
Size per entry = $6$ bytes
Total TLB size = $256 \times 6 = 1536$ bytes.

Conclusion: The size of the TLB is $1536$ bytes.

$$\boxed{1536}$$

subject: Operating System
question:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are $8$ holes in the memory of sizes $20 \mathrm{KB}, 4 \mathrm{~KB}$, $25 \mathrm{~KB}, 18 \mathrm{~KB}, 7 \mathrm{~KB}, 9 \mathrm{~KB}, 15 \mathrm{~KB}$, and $12$ KB. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes $\text{P1}$ of size $16$ KB and $\text{P2}$ of size $9$ KB arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to $\text{P1}$ and $\text{P2}$, the number of holes of size less than $8$ KB is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)
Note: $1 \mathrm{K}=2^{10}$
answer_text:
Step 1: List the initial holes.

Initial holes (in KB): 20, 4, 25, 18, 7, 9, 15, 12.

Step 2: Allocate P1 (16 KB) using best-fit.

Best-fit chooses the smallest hole that is large enough to accommodate the process.

Check each hole:
- 20 KB → can fit, remainder = 4 KB
- 4 KB → too small (4 < 16)
- 25 KB → can fit, remainder = 9 KB
- 18 KB → can fit, remainder = 2 KB
- 7 KB → too small
- 9 KB → too small
- 15 KB → too small (15 < 16)
- 12 KB → too small

The holes that can fit P1 are: 20, 25, 18. Among these, the smallest is 18 KB (remainder 2 KB).

Allocate P1 to the 18 KB hole. Remove 18 KB, add a new hole of size 2 KB (since no two holes are adjacent, this remains separate).

New hole list after P1 allocation:
20, 4, 25, 2 (from 18), 7, 9, 15, 12.

Step 3: Allocate P2 (9 KB) using best-fit.

Check each hole:
- 20 KB → can fit, remainder = 11 KB
- 4 KB → too small
- 25 KB → can fit, remainder = 16 KB
- 2 KB → too small
- 7 KB → too small
- 9 KB → can fit exactly, remainder = 0 KB (hole disappears)
- 15 KB → can fit, remainder = 6 KB
- 12 KB → can fit, remainder = 3 KB

The holes that can fit P2 are: 20, 25, 9, 15, 12. Among these, the smallest is 9 KB (exact fit, remainder 0).

Allocate P2 to the 9 KB hole. Remove that hole completely (no new hole added).

New hole list after P2 allocation:
20, 4, 25, 2, 7, 15, 12.

Step 4: Count holes of size less than 8 KB.

Holes less than 8 KB: 4 KB, 2 KB, 7 KB.

That is 3 holes.

Conclusion: The number of holes of size less than 8 KB after both allocations is 3.

$$\boxed{3}$$

The following table gives the conditional probabilities for Delhi’s temperature given Guwahati’s temperature.
$$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline & H_D & M_D & L_D \\ \hline H_G & 0.40 & 0.48 & 0.12 \\ \hline M_G & 0.10 & 0.65 & 0.25 \\ \hline L_G & 0.01 & 0.50 & 0.49 \\ \hline \end{array} $$
Consider the first row in the table above. The first entry denotes that if Guwahati has high temperature $(H_G)$ then the probability of Delhi also having a high temperature $(H_D)$ is $0.40$; i.e., $P(H_D | H_G) = 0.40$. Similarly, the next two entries are $P(M_D | H_G) = 0.48$ and $P(L_D | H_G) = 0.12$. Similarly for the other rows. If it is known that $P(H_G) = 0.2, P(M_G) = 0.5$, and $P(L_G)=0.3$, then the probability (correct to three decimal places) that Guwahati has high temperature given that Delhi has high temperature is ________.

```asm
MOV B, #0        ; B ← 0
MOV C, #8        ; C ← 8
Z:
CMP C, #0        ; Compare C with 0
JZ X             ; Jump to X if zero flag is set
SUB C, #1        ; C ← C - 1

Y:

X:
```
